title: The Sword over Jerusalem
sum: Satan stands up against Israel and stirs David to count the people. Joab objects that the count will bring guilt on Israel, but the king overrules him. The count comes back: 1,100,000 men in Israel and 470,000 in Judah, with Levi and Benjamin left out. God is displeased, David confesses, and the prophet Gad offers three punishments. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, and a plague kills seventy thousand.

As the destroying angel stretches his sword over Jerusalem, the LORD relents. David and the elders, in sackcloth, fall on their faces, and David asks God to strike him and his family instead of the sheep. At the angel's command he buys Ornan's threshing floor for six hundred shekels of gold, builds an altar, and God answers with fire from heaven. The angel sheathes his sword. Because David is too afraid to go to the tabernacle at Gibeon, this new altar becomes the place of sacrifice, and the next verse names it the site of God's house.
readings: Read beside 2 Samuel 24

Most of the chapter copies 2 Samuel 24, and the changes stand out: Satan for the LORD's anger, guilt on Israel, three years instead of seven, the angel with drawn sword, fire from heaven, and a larger price. Some changes are the Chronicler's; others, like the angel scene, seem to come from the Samuel text he used, which the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a partly preserves.
Read as the founding of the temple

Samuel ends its books with this story; Chronicles makes it the start of the temple story. A sin brings judgment, judgment is stopped by mercy, and the place where mercy met David becomes the place where Israel will seek God.

views.H: Traditional readers take the census, plague and purchase as real events late in David's reign, and both accounts as true: God allowed Satan to tempt David, and David's sin brought judgment. The Jebusite's threshing floor on the hill north of the City of David became the temple mount, and Jewish tradition identifies it with Moriah, where Isaac was bound.
views.C: Critical scholars read the chapter as the Chronicler's careful revision of 2 Samuel 24 to explain why the temple stands where it does and why its altar is legitimate though the tabernacle was at Gibeon. Many see the replacement of the LORD by Satan as a sign of later theology. The large numbers and the gold price are usually treated as the writer's enlargements.
views.S: This is one of the clearest windows into how Chronicles used Samuel. Where Chronicles agrees with 4QSam-a (the angel standing between earth and sky, the elders in sackcloth, Ornan threshing wheat) it is likely copying an older Samuel text, not inventing. Where it differs from all Samuel witnesses (Satan, guilt on Israel, fire from heaven, gold for silver, 21:28–22:1) it is likely shaping the story toward the temple.
views.J: The Talmud asks what the LORD 'saw' before relenting and answers that he saw the ashes of Isaac on this mountain (Bavli Berakhot 62b). The census is linked to the half-shekel ransom of Exodus 30:12, and the rabbis taught that Israel should not be counted head by head. The site is the Temple Mount, toward which Jews still pray.
views.X: Christians have read the chapter with Job 1–2 and James 1:13: God permits testing but does not tempt to sin. David asking to bear the punishment for his sheep is read as a picture of the good shepherd (John 10:11), and the altar where judgment stopped as a pointer to the cross, where, in Christian belief, God's judgment and mercy met.

deep.b:
Samuel says, "The LORD's anger burned against Israel once more. He stirred David up against them" (2 Samuel 24:1). Chronicles says, "Satan stood up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel" (21:1). Four main readings are held today. (1) Both are true. God allowed Satan to act, as in Job, where the satan does harm only within limits God sets (Job 1:12; 2:6), and in 1 Kings 22:19–23, where a spirit from God's council goes out to deceive Ahab. Most Christian and many Jewish interpreters have held some form of this view. (2) An earthly adversary. Because satan has no article, it may be a common noun, "an adversary." Sara Japhet leaves room for this reading, and John Sailhamer argued that the adversary was an enemy army whose threat led David to muster his troops. (3) A heavenly attacker, not the devil. Peggy Day traced satan as a role taken by different heavenly beings, and Ryan Stokes argued that the Chronicler pictured an attacking angel like the one who stood against Balaam "as an adversary" (Numbers 22:22), perhaps the same destroying angel of 21:15–16. (4) A change in theology. Many critical scholars see the Chronicler, writing after the exile, unwilling to say that God moved a king to sin, and so naming another agent; the change is often placed on a line from Job and Zechariah to the devil of later Jewish and Christian writings.

All four agree that the Chronicler did not let David off: he still says "It is I who sinned" (21:17).

Before the Dead Sea Scrolls, scholars assumed that every difference between Chronicles and Samuel was the Chronicler's own change. The Samuel scroll 4QSam-a (about 50–25 BC) changed that. In this chapter it appears to share with Chronicles the angel "standing between earth and sky" and the elders in sackcloth (21:16), Ornan threshing wheat (21:20), and perhaps "the shepherd" (21:17). Werner Lemke and Steven McKenzie argued that the Chronicler used a Samuel text of this type, so many apparent changes are really differences in the Bible he read. The scroll is fragmentary and the reconstructions are debated (see the variants on 2 Samuel 24:16 and 24:20).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the census undone
deep.b: This is my own reading, labeled as such. Chapter 21 is a count that goes wrong; chapters 23–27 are a long series of counts that go right. The Levites are "counted head by head" (23:3), the priests and singers are divided into twenty-four, and the army into twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand, all without plague. The difference, as I read it, is purpose and method: David's census in chapter 21 numbered "men who could draw a sword," the strength of the king; the later lists number people for service in God's house, and their order is set by lot, which leaves the choice to God (24:5; 25:8; 26:13). The writer seems to mark the contrast himself in 27:23–24, where he notes that David did not count those under twenty because of God's promise and that Joab's unfinished count brought wrath. So the temple, founded on the site where a forbidden count was punished, is staffed by counts made for worship. Commentators such as Japhet and Klein link 27:23–24 back to chapter 21, but I have not seen the whole of chapters 23–27 read as a deliberate reversal of the census.

echoes: 2 Samuel 24:1–25; Job 1:6–12; Job 2:1–7; Numbers 22:22–35; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 23:9; Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38; 2 Chronicles 3:1; 2 Chronicles 7:1; Sirach 2:18

settings.what: David's order to count Israel and Joab's protest
settings.to: Joab and the leaders of the people; then David
settings.when: When the adversary (satan) stirred David to count Israel
settings.why: Joab objects that the people already belong to the king, and asks, 'Why should it become guilt for Israel?' The protest shows readers that the count was wrong and that David overruled good advice. In Chronicles an adversary (satan) stands up against Israel, where 2 Samuel 24:1 has the LORD's anger.
views: Many readers: the Chronicler names the adversary to keep God from being the one who tempts David.
Others, such as Sailhamer and Stokes, read 'an adversary' (perhaps a human enemy or an angel of judgment), without the later idea of the devil.

settings.to: God
settings.when: After God struck Israel for the census
settings.why: 'This thing I have done is a great sin... Now please take away your servant's guilt. I have been a great fool.' A king confesses without excuse. For readers taught by the whole book to humble themselves and seek forgiveness (2 Chronicles 7:14), David's prayer was the first model.

settings.what: Gad's message of three choices and David's answer
settings.by: The LORD through Gad, David's visionary; then David
settings.to: David
settings.when: After David confessed his sin
settings.why: Three punishments: famine, war or plague. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, 'for his compassion runs very deep.' The answer shows trust in God's mercy even under judgment. For readers who knew judgment in the exile, it taught that the LORD's hand is safer than any human one.

settings.by: David, in sackcloth with the elders
settings.to: God
settings.when: As the angel stood with drawn sword over Jerusalem
settings.why: 'These sheep, what did they do?' David asks God to strike him and his family, not the people. A king takes the guilt on himself. The prayer leads to the angel's order to build an altar on Ornan's floor, the future Temple site. Readers saw that their Temple stood where sin was confessed and mercy given.

settings.by: The LORD's angel, through Gad the visionary
settings.to: David
settings.when: While the angel stood over Jerusalem with drawn sword
settings.why: David is to go up and build an altar on Ornan's threshing floor. The command turns a place of judgment into a place of sacrifice, and it fixes the site of the future Temple (2 Chronicles 3:1). For readers, the site of their Temple was chosen by God's word, not by a king's wish.

settings.to: Each other, at the threshing floor
settings.when: After Gad's word to build an altar there
settings.why: Ornan offers the place and everything for the offering for free; David insists on paying the full price: 'I will not... offer up a burnt offering I got for free.' The purchase makes the Temple site Israel's by right, like Abraham's purchase of Machpelah (Genesis 23). For readers living among neighbors who disputed their claims, it was a legal title to the Temple Mount.

title: A House for a Man of Rest
sum: David names the threshing floor "the house of the LORD God" and begins to prepare. He drafts the foreigners living in Israel as stonecutters and lays up iron, bronze and cedar beyond weighing or counting. Solomon is young and the house must be great, so David gets everything ready before he dies.

Then he charges Solomon. God told David he could not build because he had shed much blood; a son would be born, a man of rest, named Solomon, who would build the house, and God would be his father. David prays for wisdom for Solomon, tells him to keep the Law, and lists the enormous stores of gold and silver he has set aside. Finally he tells Israel's leaders to help Solomon, since God has given them rest, and to set their hearts on seeking the LORD and building his holy place.
readings: Read as a handover

The chapter follows the pattern of Moses handing his work to Joshua: an encouragement ("Be strong and bold"), a task, and a promise that God will be present. David, like Moses, cannot finish what he began.
Read as theology of peace
The temple belongs to rest, not war. David the warrior gathers; Solomon, whose name sounds like shalom, builds.

views.H: Traditional readers see David's real preparations, which Kings does not mention, and take the reason he could not build as both moral and ritual: the blood of war, even just war, did not suit the founder of God's house.
views.C: Most critical scholars read chapters 22–29 as the Chronicler's own composition, with no source in Samuel–Kings, giving the temple and its staff the authority of David. The vast sums of 22:14 are usually taken as deliberate hyperbole.
views.S: Kings gives the whole temple project to Solomon (1 Kings 5–7) and explains David's failure to build by his wars (1 Kings 5:3). Chronicles turns David into the temple's planner and supplier and gives a moral reason, bloodshed. 2 Samuel 7's "I will be a father to him" is applied by name to Solomon, and the warning about punishing him is left out.
views.J: Some rabbinic sources count Solomon among the few people God named before birth, citing 22:9. Jewish commentators discuss whether David's bloodshed was sinful or only unfitting; the Mishnah's rule that iron, which shortens life, may not touch the altar (Mishnah Middot 3:4) offers a parallel.
views.X: Christians read 22:10 with Hebrews 1:5, where God's words "he will be a son to me" are applied to Jesus, and see in the man of rest who builds God's house a picture of Christ, who builds his church (Matthew 16:18) and gives rest (Matthew 11:28).

deep.b: The Bible gives three answers. In 2 Samuel 7:5–7 God does not need a house: "I have never lived in a house. I have walked about in a tent" (2 Samuel 7:6). In 1 Kings 5:3 David was too busy with war. In Chronicles God says David has shed much blood (22:8; 28:3). These can be combined: David's life was war, and the temple was meant for a time of rest (22:9; Deuteronomy 12:10). Readers differ on whether the blood made David guilty, or only unsuitable, as a soldier who has killed in a just war may still be kept from certain holy tasks. The answer of Chronicles also suited its first readers, who had no king and no army, but did have a temple.

A hundred thousand talents of gold and a million talents of silver (22:14) would weigh roughly 3,400 and 34,000 metric tons. Solomon's yearly income was 666 talents of gold (1 Kings 10:14). Readers have taken the figures (1) literally, as David's accumulated plunder; (2) as rhetorical exaggeration, of a piece with "beyond weighing" and "no counting" in 22:3–4 and 22:16; or (3) as numbers swollen in copying. Most commentators, conservative and critical, now favor the second. The point is plain either way: David gave everything he could.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:5–16; 1 Kings 5:3–5; 1 Kings 8:17–19; Deuteronomy 12:9–11; Deuteronomy 31:6–8; Joshua 1:6–9; Hebrews 1:5; Ezra 3:7

settings.what: David names the place of the house
settings.to: The elders and people present at Ornan's threshing floor
settings.when: After fire from heaven answered his sacrifice
settings.why: 'This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel.' David declares the site of the future Temple, like Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:17). For readers, it was the founding word for the very place where they worshiped.

settings.to: His son Solomon
settings.when: Late in David's life, after gathering materials for the Temple
settings.why: David passes on God's word that he, a man of war, may not build, but his son, a 'man of rest,' will. He prays for Solomon's wisdom and charges him, 'Be strong and bold,' as Moses charged Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7–8). The charge makes the Temple the purpose of Solomon's reign. Readers in a time of peace under Persia heard that rest is the time to build and keep the law.

settings.to: All the leaders of Israel
settings.when: Right after his charge to Solomon
settings.why: 'Set your heart and your being to seek the LORD your God. Get up and build.' David reminds the leaders that God has given rest, and calls them to help Solomon and bring the ark into the house. The words were written for a community whose leaders were also called to support the Temple.

title: Levites for a House That Stays
sum: In old age David makes Solomon king and gathers Israel's leaders with the priests and Levites. The Levites thirty and over number thirty-eight thousand: twenty-four thousand to run the temple's work, six thousand officials and judges, four thousand gatekeepers and four thousand musicians. David divides them by Levi's three sons, Gershon, Kohath and Merari, and lists the heads of their families. Aaron's line is set apart for the most holy things; Moses' sons are counted as ordinary Levites.

Because God has given rest and lives in Jerusalem, the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle. Their new work is to help Aaron's sons: to keep the courts and rooms, clean the holy things, prepare the bread and grain offerings, check every measure, and stand morning and evening to give thanks and praise.
readings: Read as a job description
The chapter turns a wilderness tribe of porters into a temple staff. Each task listed is one the Chronicler's readers could see done in the second temple.
Read as a list of names
The names are working records, kept for assigning turns. Their gaps and repetitions (23:9–10) show their use and copying over time.

views.H: Traditional readers see David's real organization of the Levites for the coming temple, adjusting the Law of Moses to new conditions as a prophet-king could.
views.C: Many critical scholars find layers: an older list using thirty years (23:3) updated to twenty (23:24, 23:27), and a later concern to define the Levites' rank beside the priests, a live issue in the second temple period.
views.S: Samuel and Kings say almost nothing of the Levites. Chronicles fills chapters 23–27 with them, and roots their duties in David's last words.
views.J: The rabbis harmonize the different ages (Bavli Hullin 24a) and see in the morning and evening praise the origin of daily prayer at the hours of sacrifice.
views.X: Christians have read the Levites' service of praise as a pattern for church music and ministry, and Hebrews contrasts the many priests and Levites with the one priesthood of Christ (Hebrews 7:23–25).

echoes: Numbers 3:17–37; Numbers 4:1–49; Numbers 8:24–26; Deuteronomy 10:8; Leviticus 24:5–9; Numbers 28–29; Ezra 3:8

settings.to: The Levites, with all Israel's leaders and the priests gathered
settings.when: When David was old and made Solomon king
settings.why: David counts the Levites and assigns them to four kinds of work: the work of the LORD's house, officials and judges, gatekeepers and musicians. The ruling gives each group its task in the coming Temple. For readers it was the charter of the Temple staff in their own day.
views: Traditional readers: David organized the Levites as Chronicles says.
Many critical scholars: the lists of chapters 23–27 reflect the second Temple's arrangements, set back in David's day, and some think parts were added later (Williamson).

settings.what: David's ruling on the Levites' age and duties
settings.to: The Levites, from twenty years old and up
settings.when: Before the Temple was built, looking ahead to it
settings.why: Since the LORD now lives in Jerusalem, the tabernacle need not be carried. So the Levites take on new work. They help the priests, care for the courts and rooms, and cleanse the holy things. They prepare the bread and flour, keep the measures, and stand morning and evening to give thanks. Service now starts at twenty, though 23:3 counts from thirty, Numbers 4:3 has thirty and Numbers 8:24 has twenty-five. The returned exiles also appointed Levites from twenty years old (Ezra 3:8). The rule answers what Levites do once there is a fixed house, a question alive in the second Temple.

traditions.q: Do Christian ministers carry on the work of Israel's priests and Levites (1 Chronicles 23)?
views: In part, yes. The Church sees in the priesthood of Aaron and the service of the Levites a picture of the ordained ministry, which shares in the one priesthood of Christ (Catechism 1539–1541). Its prayers of ordination recall them.

The three orders of bishop, priest and deacon fulfill the pattern of high priest, priests and Levites; 1 Clement, an early Christian letter of about AD 96, already drew the comparison (chapters 40–44). At the altar the priest offers the one sacrifice of Christ.

God set up the office of preaching and giving the sacraments (Augsburg Confession 5), but it is not a sacrificing priesthood. Luther taught that all the baptized are priests (To the Christian Nobility, 1520), and the pastor serves them by a public call.

No. Christ is the last high priest, and his one offering ended the Levitical system (Hebrews 7:23–27). Every believer is a priest (1 Peter 2:9), and the church has two offices, pastor and deacon (Baptist Faith and Message 6).

title: Twenty-Four Courses
sum: Aaron's two older sons died childless, so the priests all come from Eleazar and Ithamar. With Zadok and Ahimelech, David divides them: sixteen family heads from Eleazar, eight from Ithamar. The order is drawn by lot before the king, the leaders and the scribe Shemaiah, who writes it down. Twenty-four names follow, from Jehoiarib to Maaziah, each a course with its turn to serve in the LORD's house.
The rest of the Levites are listed again, one generation further on, and they too cast lots, the senior family no different from the youngest.
readings: Read as a calendar
The twenty-four courses made a rotation, a week at a time, that lasted until the temple fell in AD 70. Zechariah of the course of Abijah was on duty when the angel appeared to him (Luke 1:5–9).

views.H: Traditional readers credit David with the twenty-four-course system, which Josephus, the Mishnah and the New Testament assume was ancient.
views.C: Many scholars date the full system after the exile: Nehemiah's lists of priestly families (Nehemiah 12:1–21) have fewer names, some the same, and Williamson argued that this chapter reflects its growth in the Persian period.
views.S: Nothing in Samuel or Kings corresponds. The pairing of Zadok with Ahimelech son of Abiathar repeats the confusion of 2 Samuel 8:17.
views.J: The Mishnah pairs each priestly course with a lay delegation, the ma'amad (Mishnah Taanit 4:2). After AD 70 the courses were remembered in synagogue poems and inscriptions, like the one from Caesarea.
views.X: Luke's story of John the Baptist's birth opens inside this system. Revelation's twenty-four elders have often been linked with the twenty-four courses.

deep.b: Nehemiah lists priestly families that returned from exile (Nehemiah 12:1–7, 12:12–21), many with names from this chapter. Mattathias, father of the Maccabees, was of the first course, Jehoiarib (1 Maccabees 2:1). Josephus, a priest of the same course, says the system lasted to his day (Life 1–2; Antiquities 7.365–366). The Qumran community kept calendars of the courses (4Q320–330). After the temple fell, the courses' families were remembered by town; an inscription from Caesarea lists them with their homes in Galilee.

echoes: Leviticus 10:1–2; Numbers 3:4; Nehemiah 12:1–21; 1 Maccabees 2:1; Luke 1:5–9; Revelation 4:4

settings.by: David, with Zadok and Ahimelech; the lot drawn before the king and leaders
settings.to: The priests, the descendants of Aaron through Eleazar and Ithamar
settings.when: Late in David's reign
settings.why: The priests are divided by lot into twenty-four families, each serving in its turn in the Temple. The lot keeps the order fair between the two lines. These divisions were in use in the second Temple (Luke 1:5 names Abijah's, the eighth). For readers, the list told each priestly family when and by what right it served. The other Levites cast lots the same way, the head family the same as the youngest (24:20–31).

title: Prophets with Lyres
sum: David and the army commanders set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals. Four sons of Asaph, six of Jeduthun and fourteen of Heman, the king's visionary, lead the music. All 288 trained singers, twenty-four groups of twelve, draw lots for their turns, teacher and pupil alike.
readings: Read as worship
The singers' praise is called prophecy: music in God's house speaks for God and to God.
Read as a poem in a list
The names of Heman's last nine sons, read in a row, sound like the lines of a psalm (see the note on 25:4).

views.H: Traditional readers take the guilds of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun as David's own creation and the psalms bearing their names as their work.
views.C: Many critical scholars see the singers of the Chronicler's day, whose rank rose in the second temple, claiming David's authority and the prophets' authority for their office.
views.S: Samuel mentions David's music but not temple guilds; Chronicles develops them here and in 15:16–24 and 16:4–42.
views.J: The Levites sang a fixed psalm for each day of the week in the temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4).
views.X: Christians see in the prophet-musicians a basis for sung worship, and in 'psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit' (Colossians 3:16) a continuation of their work.

echoes: 1 Samuel 10:5; 2 Kings 3:15; Psalm 50; Psalm 73–83; Psalm 88; 2 Chronicles 5:12–14; 2 Chronicles 29:25–30; 2 Chronicles 35:15

settings.what: The singers and their twenty-four turns
settings.to: The sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, the Temple singers
settings.when: Late in David's reign
settings.why: The singers 'prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals,' and are divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve. Calling their music prophecy gave the Levite singers great honor, and the list says their place came from David himself. For readers whose Temple choirs were Levites, it was the root of their office.
views: Many scholars see the Chronicler giving the Levite singers a prophetic role, perhaps because prophets had grown rare (Petersen).
Others: 'prophesied' means inspired praise, not new oracles.

traditions.q: David set apart musicians with lyres, harps and cymbals for worship (1 Chronicles 25:1). Should churches use instruments?
views: The Byzantine and Slavic churches sing their services with the human voice alone, as the early church did. Many Orthodox teachers treat the temple's instruments as part of the old worship that has passed.
The Ethiopian church worships with drums, sistrums and prayer staffs, and its church singers (debteras) dance before the tabot, the copy of the ark, as David danced before the ark of the LORD.
Luther loved music and gave it the highest place after theology. Lutheran churches made the organ and the choir central to worship, as in the music of Bach, and read David's musicians as a model.

Calvin taught that instruments belonged to the time of the Law, like the temple and its sacrifices, and that Christians should praise God with the voice (Commentary on Psalms, on Psalm 33:2). Many Presbyterian churches long sang only psalms, unaccompanied; most now use instruments, and the Free Church of Scotland allowed them only in 2010.

Churches of Christ sing without instruments. They teach that the New Testament commands singing (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16) and never names instruments for the church, and that David's instruments belonged to the covenant Christ fulfilled. Other Restorationist bodies, such as the Christian Churches, use them.

Pentecostal worship welcomes bands, drums and every kind of instrument, with Psalm 150 and David's musicians as models. Many link the musicians who prophesied with lyres (1 Chronicles 25:1–3) to worship in which the Spirit speaks.

title: Keepers of the Gates and the Treasures
sum: The gatekeepers come from Korah's line, through Meshelemiah, and from Obed-edom, whom God blessed with many sons, and from Hosah of Merari. Lots assign the gates: east, north, south with the storehouse, west by the Shallecheth Gate, with guard posts set day by day.

Other Levites keep the treasuries, among them the dedicated plunder of Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and David. Still others serve outside the temple as officials and judges, and Hebronite Levites oversee the tribes on both sides of the Jordan for every matter of God and of the king.

views.H: Traditional readers see David's provision for every part of the temple's life, including its security and its finances.
views.C: Critical scholars see the gatekeepers and treasurers of the second temple, whose families and posts are traced back to David. The Persian-looking word Parbar (26:18) may point to the writer's own setting.
views.S: Samuel's Obed-edom the Gittite, who kept the ark (2 Samuel 6:10–12), becomes a Levite patriarch here. Samuel and Kings know of dedicated plunder (2 Samuel 8:11) but not of these treasurers.
views.J: The Mishnah describes the night watches of priests and Levites at the gates of the second temple and names its gates (Mishnah Middot 1:1–4); Psalm 84, with its wish to stand at the threshold of God's house, is a psalm of the sons of Korah.
views.X: Christians have taken the gatekeepers as a picture of humble service in God's house (Psalm 84:10) and of watchfulness.

echoes: Numbers 16; Numbers 26:11; 2 Samuel 6:10–12; 9:17–27; Psalm 84:10; 2 Kings 23:11; 2 Chronicles 19:8–11

settings.by: David; the lots cast family by family
settings.to: The gatekeepers of the Korahite and Merarite families
settings.when: Late in David's reign
settings.why: Each family is given a gate by lot, with a set number of guards a day. The gatekeepers kept the unclean out of the holy place. For readers, gatekeepers were a real office in the second Temple (Nehemiah 11:19), and the list placed them in David's order.

settings.to: Levites assigned to the treasuries and to work outside the Temple
settings.when: Late in David's reign, in his fortieth year
settings.why: Levites guard the treasuries of holy gifts, including gifts from Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab. Others serve as officials and judges across Israel 'for every matter of God and every matter of the king.' The list ties Temple wealth and local justice to the Levites, a role they still had in the readers' time.

title: The King's Army and Estate
sum: Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men each serve the king a month at a time, led by commanders whose names match David's heroes. The leaders of the tribes follow, then a note that David did not count those under twenty, since God promised Israel would be like the stars, and that Joab's count was never finished. Twelve stewards manage the king's treasuries, farms, vineyards, oil, herds, camels and flocks. Last come the king's counselors: Jonathan, Ahithophel, Hushai, Jehoiada, Abiathar and Joab.

views.H: Traditional readers see a real administrative record from David's later reign, preserved in royal archives.
views.C: Many scholars see an idealized scheme, built on the names of 11:10–47 and on twelve months, with Asahel's presence (27:7) as a sign that it was not a roster from one moment. The stewards' list (27:25–31) is often thought more likely to rest on an old record.
views.S: Samuel has lists of David's officials (2 Samuel 8:15–18; 20:23–26) and heroes (2 Samuel 23:8–39), but not this militia or the stewards.
views.J: The Talmud reads 27:34 as a picture of how David decided matters: Ahithophel gave counsel, "Jehoiada son of Benaiah" stands for the court, Abiathar for the Urim and Thummim, and Joab for the army (Bavli Berakhot 3b–4a). The phrase divre hayyamim in 27:24 is the Hebrew name of the book.
views.X: Christian readers have used the chapter as a picture of an ordered kingdom, every gift in its place (1 Corinthians 12:28).

settings.what: David's army divisions, tribal leaders and officials
settings.to: The Chronicler's readers
settings.when: David's reign
settings.why: Twelve divisions serve a month each, every tribe has its leader, and stewards run the king's lands. The order of the kingdom matches the order of the Temple. The note that David did not count those under twenty, and that Joab's count was never finished (27:23–24), recalls the sin of chapter 21. Readers saw a well-ordered Israel, all twelve tribes in place.

title: The Pattern from God's Hand
sum: David gathers all Israel's leaders and stands to speak. He had set his heart on building a resting house for the ark, God's footstool, but God said a man of wars could not build it. God chose Judah, David's family, David himself, and now Solomon to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom and build his house, if he keeps God's commands. David charges the assembly and Solomon: know God, serve him with a whole heart, seek him and he will be found.

Then David hands Solomon the pattern of the temple: porch, rooms, treasuries, the room for the atonement lid, the courses of priests and Levites, the weight of gold and silver for every vessel, and the chariot of the cherubim. "All of it is in writing, from the LORD's hand on me." He ends as Moses ended with Joshua: be strong and bold, God will not abandon you.
readings: Read as a second Sinai
As God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle, he gives David the pattern of the temple. The temple is not Solomon's design but God's.
Read as a testament
Like Moses' farewell in Deuteronomy, David's last speeches mix history, charge, warning and promise.

views.H: Traditional readers take 28:19 as real revelation: David received a written plan by inspiration, as Moses did.
views.C: Critical scholars read the plan as the Chronicler's way of grounding the second temple's order in David's authority. The chapter's language is close to Deuteronomy and Joshua.
views.S: 1 Kings 1 shows a bedridden David; here he stands before an assembly. 1 Kings 2:1–4 has a private charge to Solomon; Chronicles makes it public and adds the pattern.
views.J: Jewish readers note that 28:18 is the first place the cherubim are called a 'chariot' (merkavah), the word later used for teaching about God's throne, which the Mishnah allowed only to the wise (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1).
views.X: Hebrews 8:5 reads the tabernacle pattern as a copy of the heavenly sanctuary; Christians read David's pattern the same way. 28:9's promise, 'seek him, and he will let you find him', is echoed by Jesus (Matthew 7:7).

deep.h: "From the LORD's hand": history or the writer's time?
deep.b: David says the whole plan came "in writing, from the LORD's hand on me" (28:19). Readers weigh this differently. As history: God gave David a plan as he gave Moses one (Exodus 25:9, 25:40), and the temple was built to it; the claim matches the Bible's view that worship must follow God's design. As inspired design: "the LORD's hand" is the prophets' phrase for being seized by God (Ezekiel 1:3; 2 Kings 3:15), so David drew the plan under inspiration, and "in writing" means he wrote it down. As the Chronicler's claim: many critical scholars think the writer, living in the Persian period, used David's authority to support the temple order of his own day, its Levite courses, singers and gatekeepers. These are not wholly exclusive: one may hold that David did plan the temple and also that the Chronicler presents that plan with an eye on his readers.

echoes: Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Deuteronomy 31:6–8; Joshua 1:5–9; Psalm 132:7–8; 1 Kings 2:1–4; 1 Kings 6–7; Hebrews 8:5

settings.to: All Israel's leaders gathered in Jerusalem: tribal leaders, commanders, stewards, palace officials and warriors; then Solomon
settings.when: At the end of David's reign
settings.why: David tells the story of the Temple. He wished to build a resting house for the ark, but God refused because he was a man of war. God chose Judah, then David, then Solomon to sit 'on the throne of the LORD's kingdom.' He charges the assembly to keep the commands so they can keep the good land, and Solomon to 'know your father's God.' The speech is written for a later assembly too: the land, the Temple and God's kingdom are kept by seeking him.
views: Traditional readers: a record of David's last address, preserved in the prophets' records (29:29).
Many scholars, following von Rad, read the speeches of Chronicles as sermons in a Levitical style, written for the Chronicler's own hearers.

settings.what: The pattern of the Temple, in writing
settings.by: David, from 'the LORD's hand on me'
settings.to: Solomon his son
settings.when: At the same assembly
settings.why: David gives Solomon a written plan for every room, every division of priests and Levites, and the weight of every vessel. 'All of it is in writing, from the LORD's hand.' Like the pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9), it says the Temple was God's design, not a king's. For readers it gave their worship divine authority.

settings.to: Solomon
settings.when: At the same assembly
settings.why: 'Be strong and bold... He will not let you down.' The words echo Moses to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:6–8) and promise that priests, Levites, craftsmen and leaders are all ready. They encouraged any generation facing a great work for God.

title: Yours Is the Kingdom
sum: David tells the assembly that the work is great and the citadel is for God, lists what he has prepared, and gives his own private treasure of gold and silver. He asks who else will give, and the leaders give freely: gold, darics, silver, bronze, iron and precious stones. The people rejoice at their own giving.

Then David blesses the LORD before the assembly in a prayer of praise: greatness, might, beauty, victory and majesty belong to God, and the kingdom too. Everything comes from God's hand; Israel are foreigners and lodgers whose days are a shadow. He prays that God will keep the people's hearts true and give Solomon a whole heart. The assembly worships, offers a thousand bulls, rams and lambs, eats and drinks, and makes Solomon king a second time, with Zadok as priest. Solomon sits on the LORD's throne, all Israel obeys him, and David dies at a good old age. His deeds are written by Samuel, Nathan and Gad.
readings: Read as worship
The chapter moves from giving to praise to sacrifice to a feast: a model of worship in which gifts are returned to the God who gave them.
Read as a farewell
David's last words are a prayer, not a command. The book ends with his peaceful death, satisfied with days like Abraham.

views.H: Traditional readers see David's real farewell, the gifts and the prayer, and a peaceful transfer of power; the darics are the writer's updating of the money.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the prayer as the Chronicler's composition, in the style of the prayers of Ezra 9 and Nehemiah 9, and see the darics (29:7) and the word birah (29:1) as signs of the Persian period. The sums are usually read as hyperbole.
views.S: 1 Kings 1–2 tells of Adonijah's attempt, David's instructions to deal with Joab and Shimei, and his death. Chronicles leaves out the conflict, has all David's sons pledge loyalty, and ends with an anointing before the assembly. 29:26–27 follows 1 Kings 2:11 nearly word for word.
views.J: 29:10–13 is recited every morning in the synagogue (Vayevarekh David), and 29:11 is sung as the Torah scroll is carried. The five nouns of 29:11 gave names to the sefirot of Kabbalah. The Talmud names Samuel, Gad and Nathan as the writers of the book of Samuel (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a).
views.X: The doxology many Christians add to the Lord's Prayer, 'For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever', is modeled on 29:11; it is not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew 6:13 but appears in an early form in the Didache. 29:14 is used at the offering in many churches, and 29:15 stands behind Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11.

deep.h: David's prayer and the Lord's Prayer
deep.b: David's prayer has four movements: blessing (29:10), praise of God's greatness and kingdom (29:11–13), confession that all gifts come from God and human life is brief (29:14–16), and petition for the people and for Solomon (29:17–19). The second movement became, by way of the church's worship, the closing doxology of the Lord's Prayer. The oldest Greek manuscripts of Matthew (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) end at "deliver us from evil"; the Didache, a church manual of about AD 100, adds "for yours is the power and the glory forever"; later manuscripts add "the kingdom" too, and the King James Version prints it. Most scholars think the line was added for public worship, following the Jewish custom of ending prayers with praise, and that David's words here were its model. Defenders of the Byzantine text, such as Maurice Robinson, dissent and hold that the doxology belongs to Matthew's original.

deep.h: Darics and the date of Chronicles
deep.b: The adarkon (29:7) is almost certainly the daric, a gold coin introduced by the Persian king Darius I around 515 BC, though some link the word with the Greek drachma. Coins did not exist in David's time. The writer is giving the value in money his readers used, as a modern writer might convert an ancient sum to dollars. For dating, the word means that Chronicles was written after darics had become common, which most scholars place in the 400s or 300s BC. Together with the word birah, "citadel" (29:1), and the genealogy of David's line that runs well past the return from exile (3:17–24), it supports the common view that the book comes from the Persian or early Greek period. Traditional readers who hold that Ezra wrote Chronicles (Bavli Bava Batra 15a) agree: Ezra lived under Persian rule, and he mentions darics himself (Ezra 8:27).

echoes: 1 Kings 1–2; 1 Kings 2:10–12; Exodus 35:21–29; Exodus 36:5–7; Leviticus 25:23; Psalm 39:12; Matthew 6:13; Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11; Ezra 8:27

settings.to: The whole assembly
settings.when: After his charge to Solomon
settings.why: David lists what he has prepared, gives his own private treasure, and asks, 'Who will freely give today?' The leaders and people answer with joy. The appeal is a model of leaders giving first and others following. For readers it recalled the free giving for the second Temple (Ezra 2:68–69) and called them to keep giving.

settings.to: The LORD, God of Israel, before the whole assembly
settings.when: After the people's free giving
settings.why: 'Yours, LORD, is the kingdom.' David praises God as the source of all wealth and power. He confesses that 'we are foreigners before you, and lodgers.' He prays that God will keep the people's hearts steady and give Solomon a whole heart. For readers who were a small people under a great empire, the prayer said that the kingdom is God's, whoever sits on earthly thrones. The doxology added to the Lord's Prayer is often traced to 29:11.

settings.what: David's call to bless the LORD
settings.to: The whole assembly
settings.when: At the end of his prayer
settings.why: 'Please bless the LORD your God.' The assembly answers by bowing before the LORD and the king. The book ends its David story with worship led by the king, the pattern the Chronicler wanted his readers to keep.
